conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Patel, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—you may hear it referred to as the **EPDS**. It’s just ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and experiences over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we’re just gathering information so we can best support you.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team. If at any point you need a break or want to clarify something, please let me know. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally—no paperwork on your end—and we’ll go at your pace.

Let’s begin. Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly joke—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. A lot of the time I’m just tired or distracted, so even when something’s funny, I feel like I’m faking it more than really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced. Like, I’ll smile at something silly the baby does, but the joy doesn’t last. Mostly I’m just worn out, so even when I try to find things funny, it feels kind of flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes I do look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like I’m going through the motions than really anticipating them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I think, “Maybe I’m just not good at this,” even when my head knows babies cry. It’s not every minute, but a couple of times this week I’ve felt like little hiccups were somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly I’m okay, but every now and then my mind jumps to the worst—like if she sneezes I’ll suddenly worry she’s getting really sick, even though there’s no fever or anything. It passes pretty fast once I tell myself she’s fine, but it pops up out of nowhere a couple of times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky… more like a quick flutter of “what-if” that fades once I take a breath. Nothing that feels like a real scare, just little surges that settle once I check on the baby and see she’s okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. It’s not constant, but when she won’t nap or I’m trying to get dinner started and she starts crying, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually manage to get through it, but it feels like I’m just barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Sleep’s actually been one of the better parts—once I finally lie down I’m out pretty quick. It’s just that sometimes it takes me a while to fall asleep because my mind keeps replaying the day or worrying I forgot something, but once I’m asleep I stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel kind of down some days. It’s not all the time, but I’ll catch myself feeling weepy for no real reason—like yesterday I just started crying while folding laundry. It lifts after a bit, but the sadness keeps popping back up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That happened a couple of times this week—nothing huge set me off, just suddenly felt overwhelmed and the tears came. It wasn’t all day, but yeah, I did cry once or twice when the feelings just bubbled over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and teary, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

You've shared how the last week has felt like wading through fog-smiling when you know you should, yet the joy quickly slips away, replaced by fatigue and self-doubt. Moments of laughter with your partner or pride in your baby are followed by sudden tears while folding laundry, and worries about her health surge even when all seems fine. You're working hard to stay afloat, telling yourself these feelings will pass, but the sadness and pressure keep bubbling up, leaving you wondering when you'll feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can still laugh but describes it as forced, fleeting, and flat—matching "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient's description of diminished excitement and "going through the motions" aligns semantically with "Definitely less than I used to," indicating noticeably reduced enjoyment.</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a couple of times this week" and links baby's fussiness to personal inadequacy, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Frequent, intrusive worry episodes several times daily without medical basis map to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes intermittent overwhelm ('some days') and feeling like 'drowning' yet still managing, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>"quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 14 places you above the ≥14 cutoff indicating high likelihood of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You describe core symptoms-depressed mood most days, greatly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent anxiety-present nearly every day for the past week. These map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> (≥5 symptoms, same two-week period). Absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring, yet functional impact (<quote>barely keeping my head above water</quote>) warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days for full diagnostic assessment
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>, and discuss whether antidepressant medication is appropriate
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress after interventions begin
4. Reach out today to supports-partner, family, or trusted friend-and share how you're feeling; enlist help with night feeds or household tasks to secure 4-5 hours of uninterrupted rest
5. Practice brief self-care: 10-minute outdoor walk with baby most days, balanced snacks every 3-4 hours, and 5 slow belly-breaths when worries spike
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and anxiety levels to review with your provider
7. If thoughts of self-harm ever emerge, treat it as an emergency: call 911, go to your nearest ED, or contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
8. Continue routine postpartum visits and remind your clinician that EPDS screening indicates urgent concern
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ____________

Patient-reported symptoms (endorsed within past 7 days):

1. Persistent low/flat mood with episodic tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
2. Markedly diminished enjoyment ("going through the motions"; joy feels forced) (Q1, Q2)  
3. Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant-care challenges (Q3)  
4. Recurrent, intrusive "what-if" worries about infant safety; brief surges of physiological anxiety subsiding with reassurance (Q4, Q5)  
5. Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/drowning during daily tasks (Q6)  
6. Sleep-onset delay due to ruminating/worry; no middle/terminal insomnia reported (Q7)

Negative safety screen: Denies any thoughts of self-harm (Q10).

Pattern summary: Symptoms cluster consistent with mild-to-moderate postpartum depressive features with co-occurring anxiety; functional impact described as "barely keeping head above water." Onset appears within first months post-delivery; no psychotic, manic, or self-harm features elicited.

Screening significance: Elevated risk for postpartum depression and anxiety; further clinical evaluation (EPDS scoring, structured interview) recommended to confirm severity and inform level of care.
